newsitem.title: GERMANY: France, Germany to press ahead with spy satellites.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany to press ahead with spy satellites.

text.p: France and Germany averted a possible showdown over an ambitious European spy satellite programme on Friday by agreeing to go ahead with it, but at different speeds.

Meeting at their countries' six-monthly summit in Nuremberg, defence ministers Charles Millon of France and Volker Ruehe of Germany reaffirmed their support for the Helios II and Horus satellites to make Europe independent of U.S. intelligence.

Officials said France would start building Helius II next year but Germany, where spending cuts to meet the criteria for the European Union's single currency have hit the defence budget hard, will put off joining the project until 1998.

The ministers, meeting parallel to talks between French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in the mediaeval city, said in a statement this kept the joint satellite plans on target.
"The German and French defence and security council has confirmed its political will to realise the programmes according to the goals set by both countries," they said.
Officials said the ministers also agreed to move ahead in joint projects for two helicopters and a new anti-tank rocket.

France has been especially keen to build the Helios II satellite to make Europe independent of Washington's superior "spy in the sky" capabiities. It has made the project a symbol of Europe's drive for its own defence identity.

But the project, which enjoys the political backing of Kohl and Chirac, threatened to fall foul of Bonn's budget problems. Ruehe, whose thinking is closer to that of Washington and NATO, said openly he did not have the funds to build it.

Officials said Bonn must find extra funds outside Ruehe's budget to provide the seven billion marks ($4.5 billion) for its share of the Helios II and get parliamentary approval before actually joining the French in building it.
Bonn is due to fund 10 percent of the project.
On the other projects, the two sides agreed that Germany would buy a total of 212 Tiger attack helicopters while France would take 215, officials said.
Production contracts would be signed soon and each side would first order 80 apiece, they said.
On the NH90 transport helicopter being developed with Italy and the Netherlands, Germany will order 243 and France 160, they said.
Ruehe and Millon agreed in principle to order 6,000 of the new PARS-3 LR anti-tank rocket for the Tiger helicopter, they added.

The officials reported less progress with other projects like a new transport aircraft, for which France has cut its funding, and the GTK armoured transport vehicle, which Germany is developing with Britain and hopes to win French support for. ($1=1.5522 Mark)
